title: Validate protocol token spelling before lossy numeric conversion
applies_when: A protocol constrains the spelling of an index or number, but the implementation parses it with a more permissive host-language conversion and validates only the resulting value.
lesson: Separate lexical validity from numeric range. Python int() maps '-0', '+0' and '00' to the same zero, accepts surrounding whitespace and Unicode decimal digits, and therefore loses distinctions required by JSON Pointer array-index syntax. A post-conversion negative-value check rejects -1 but cannot reject signed zero. Check the decoded array token against the protocol grammar before conversion, then check bounds. Include invalid spellings whose parsed values are in range; otherwise an out-of-range failure can hide the lexical gap. Keep object-member lookup separate: keys literally named '-0', '+1' or '01' are valid strings and must not be normalized or rejected by an array-only rule.
avoid_when: General numeric APIs may deliberately accept signs, whitespace or Unicode digits; do not impose JSON Pointer grammar on them. Percent-encoding, token unescaping and container type must be resolved under their own contracts. This evidence covers native Windows CPython 3.14.3 with exact referencing source trees and existing attrs/rpds dependencies, not a proposed repair, full upstream suite, Linux portability, security impact or performance. Related lexical cases were already publicly reported; independent confirmation is not a new bug or a prospective Scout utility result.

evidence.note: Normative array-index grammar permits ASCII zero or a nonzero ASCII digit followed by ASCII digits; object-member names have a different lookup rule. This is a protocol requirement, not a universal int() contract.
Pinned other-author proposed implementation converts with int() before checking segment < 0, preserving the signed-zero and other noncanonical in-range cases. No repair is asserted here.

Independent public-API comparison: 18 decoded tokens x array/object x exact baseline/candidate = 72 observations. Candidate rejects -1/-2 but still resolves nine noncanonical in-range array spellings; all object-string and valid-index controls remain. Candidate's 114 core tests pass. Contributed a scoped review to the existing author, not a competing PR.
